summary: Jordi Galí's 2018 Journal of Economic Perspectives article takes stock of New Keynesian economics a decade after the 2007 financial crisis. It argues the New Keynesian model remains the dominant framework in teaching, research and policy modeling despite criticism of DSGE models. The paper reviews key insights, discusses recent work on the zero lower bound and on monetary policy with household heterogeneity, and outlines main shortcomings and future research areas.
one_line: Jordi Galí's 2018 review assessing the state of New Keynesian economics, its zero lower bound and household heterogeneity research, and its shortcomings.
key_facts: The article was published in the Journal of Economic Perspectives, vol. 32, no. 3, Summer 2018, pages 87-112.
The author is Jordi Galí and the DOI is 10.1257/jep.32.3.87.
The abstract says that in August 2007 the New Keynesian paradigm was dominant in macroeconomics, when the first signs of the most damaging global financial crisis since the Great Depression emerged.
The abstract states that ten years later, criticisms have been directed at modern macroeconomics and at dynamic stochastic general equilibrium models built on the New Keynesian framework.
The abstract argues the New Keynesian model arguably remains the dominant framework in the classroom, in academic research, and in policy modeling.
The scope of New Keynesian economics has kept widening over the past ten years, encompassing more phenomena and addressing some criticisms raised against it.
The paper discusses two very active research programs: the implications of the zero lower bound on nominal interest rates and the interaction of monetary policy and household heterogeneity.
The paper ends by discussing what the author views as some of the main shortcomings of the New Keynesian model and possible areas for future research.
The article's JEL classification codes include D11, E12, E31, E32, E52, E62 and G01.
The article is available as a complimentary full-text PDF from the American Economic Association website.
